usage: 한국 + 사람 stacks as a noun phrase; no particle between them
살다 takes 에 for the place of residence, not 에서
에서 marks the origin point of movement with 오다
한국 modifies 음식 directly; means cuisine of Korea
examples: 저는 한국 사람이에요.
I am Korean.
Simplest self-introduction; 한국 + 사람 + 이에요 with no particle inside the noun phrase
저는 작년에 한국에 갔어요.
I went to Korea last year.
Everyday past sentence; 가다 takes destination 에, and 왔어요 would need 에서 for origin instead
한국에서 삼 년 동안 일했는데 정말 좋았어요.
I worked in Korea for three years and it was really great.
Real-situation; 에서 marks where the activity happened, 동안 marks the span
nuance: 한국 (韓國, 'Han nation') is the short, everyday name South Koreans use for their own country; the full official name is 대한민국 (大韓民國), which you mainly hear in formal contexts, news, and at sporting events ('대한민국!' chants). The key boundary for learners: 한국 by itself almost always means South Korea, NOT the whole peninsula — North Korea is 북한 (北韓, 'north Han') and you must never call it 한국. A second near-synonym is 우리나라 ('our country'), which Koreans use warmly when speaking among themselves to mean 'Korea' from an insider stance — but a foreigner saying 우리나라 sounds odd unless they identify as Korean, so as a learner stick with 한국. The particle trap: with movement verbs, 가다/오다 destinations take 에 (한국에 가요 = go to Korea), while origin and the location of an action take 에서 (한국에서 왔어요 = came from Korea; 한국에서 살아요 is also heard but residence more strictly prefers 한국에 살아요).

mistakes: Saying 한국에 왔어요 to mean 'I came FROM Korea' — 에 marks a destination, so this means 'I came TO Korea'; for origin use 한국에서 왔어요.
Calling North Korea 한국 — 한국 means South Korea only; North Korea is 북한, and conflating them can be politically sensitive.

usage: 미국 + 사람 with no linking particle; the casual term for an American
에서 marks the country of origin with 오다
가다 takes destination 에, not 에서
미국 modifies 영화 directly; means a film made in the US
examples: 저는 미국에서 왔어요.
I came from the USA.
Simple origin sentence; 에서 marks where you came from
제 친구가 미국에 살고 있어요.
My friend is living in the USA.
Everyday; 살다 uses location 에, and 고 있다 adds the ongoing 'currently living' sense
미국에서 대학을 다녔는데 학비가 정말 비쌌어요.
I attended university in the USA and tuition was really expensive.
Real-situation; 에서 marks the location of the activity, 다니다 = attend regularly
nuance: 미국 (美國, literally 'beautiful country') is the standard Korean name for the United States, and crucially it does NOT come from the English sound 'America' — it is a Sino-Korean reading borrowed via Chinese, where 美 was chosen as a phonetic match for the 'me' in 'America' (the same character also means 'beautiful', so the name is a happy accident, not literal praise). Learners often reach for 아메리카, which Koreans understand but sounds like the continent or a textbook transliteration, not a country; in real speech everyone says 미국. The same 國 ('country') element appears in 한국, 중국, 영국 — recognizing it helps you read country names. Note that 미국 covers the whole nation, so for a specific state you must name it (예: 캘리포니아). Particle-wise it behaves like any country noun: 미국에 가다 (go to), 미국에서 오다/살다 (come from / live in). Don't confuse the country 미국 with the language: Americans speak 영어, not '미국어' — there is no such word, since the language is English.

usage: 중국 + 사람 with no particle; the casual word for a Chinese national
에서 marks the country of origin
중국 + 어 = the Chinese language; 를 marks it as the object
examples: 저는 중국에서 왔어요.
I came from China.
Simple origin sentence with 에서
중국 음식을 자주 먹어요.
I often eat Chinese food.
Everyday; 을 marks the object, 자주 = often
중국에서 이 년 동안 중국어를 공부했어요.
I studied Chinese in China for two years.
Real-situation; 에서 marks the location, and note 중국어 (language) is distinct from 중국 (country)
nuance: 중국 (中國, 'central / middle country') is the everyday Korean name for China — the hanja literally means 'the central kingdom', the name China has historically used for itself. Because China shares a long border and deep history with Korea, the word turns up constantly in daily conversation. The crucial learner split is country vs. language: 중국 is the country, but the language is 중국어 (中國語, 'China-language') — adding 어 (語, 'language/speech') turns most country names into language names (중국→중국어, 일본→일본어, 프랑스→프랑스어). English speakers habitually drop the 어 and say '중국을 배워요' ('I learn China'), which is wrong; you must say 중국어를 배워요. A person from China is 중국 사람 (casual) or 중국인 (formal, 中國人). Particle behavior is the standard country pattern: 중국에 가다 (go to), 중국에서 오다/살다 (come from / live in). Don't confuse 중국 with 중국집, which colloquially means a Korean-Chinese restaurant — a different, food-specific word.

usage: 일본 + 사람 with no particle; casual term for a Japanese national
에서 marks the country of origin
일본 modifies 여행; a trip to Japan
examples: 저는 일본 사람이에요.
I am Japanese.
Simple self-introduction; 일본 + 사람 + 이에요
다음 달에 일본에 여행 가요.
I'm going on a trip to Japan next month.
Everyday; 가다 takes destination 에, 여행 가다 = go traveling
일본에서 친구를 만나서 같이 온천에 갔어요.
I met a friend in Japan and we went to a hot spring together.
Real-situation; 에서 marks where the meeting happened, 만나다 takes 를 for the person met
nuance: 일본 (日本, 'sun-origin') is the standard Korean name for Japan — the hanja literally means 'origin of the sun' (the same characters Japan reads as 'Nihon/Nippon'), the source of the English nickname 'Land of the Rising Sun'. For Koreans, Japan is the most popular nearby overseas destination, so 일본 여행 is an extremely common phrase. The reliable learner split is country vs. language: 일본 is the country, the language is 일본어 (日本語) — add 어 and never say '일본을 공부해요' to mean 'study Japanese' (that means studying the country); say 일본어를 공부해요. A Japanese person is 일본 사람 (casual) or 일본인 (formal). One pronunciation pitfall: learners sometimes pronounce it 'il-bon' with a hard split, but the natural flow is closer to 'ilbon' with the ㄹ and ㅂ blending smoothly. Particle behavior is the usual country pattern: 일본에 가다 (go to), 일본에서 오다 (come from), 일본에서 만나다 (meet in). Don't confuse the meeting verb's particle: you meet a person with 를/을 (친구를 만나다), and the place uses 에서.

usage: 영국 + 사람 with no particle; means a person from the UK
에서 marks the country of origin
살다 takes location 에 for residence
영국 modifies 영어; the British variety of English
examples: 저는 영국에서 왔어요.
I came from the UK.
Simple origin sentence with 에서
영국은 비가 자주 와요.
It rains often in the UK.
Everyday; 은 marks 영국 as the topic, 비가 오다 = rain falls
영국에서 일 년 동안 어학연수를 했어요.
I did a year of language study in the UK.
Real-situation; 에서 marks the location, 어학연수 = language-study abroad
nuance: 영국 (英國) is the Korean name for the United Kingdom AS A WHOLE — not just England. The hanja 英 was a phonetic pick for the 'Eng-' in 'England', and the same 英 sits inside 영어 (英語, 'English language'), which is why the country and the language look related. This creates the classic learner trap: 영국 and 영어 are different words — 영국 is the country (the UK), 영어 is the English language, so 'I study English' is 영어를 공부해요, never '영국을 공부해요'. A second, subtler pitfall for English speakers is scope: in English you might distinguish England, Scotland, Wales, and Britain, but Korean 영국 lumps the whole UK together, so a Scottish person is still 영국 사람 in ordinary speech (you'd specify 스코틀랜드 only if it matters). A British person is 영국 사람 (casual) or 영국인 (formal). Particle behavior follows the country pattern: 영국에 가다/살다 (go to / live in), 영국에서 오다 (come from). Don't say '잉글랜드' as the default country word — Koreans use 영국 for the nation; 잉글랜드 mainly comes up in football/soccer contexts.

usage: 프랑스 + 사람 with no particle; means a person from France
에서 marks the country of origin
examples: 저는 프랑스에서 왔어요.
I came from France.
Simple origin sentence with 에서
프랑스 빵이 정말 맛있어요.
French bread is really delicious.
Everyday; 프랑스 modifies 빵, 맛있다 = be tasty
프랑스에서 일 년 동안 요리를 배웠어요.
I studied cooking in France for one year.
Real-situation; 에서 marks the location, 요리를 배우다 = learn cooking
nuance: 프랑스 is unusual among these country names: it is written purely phonetically from the country's own name (France), NOT with hanja like 한국·중국·미국·영국·일본·독일 — so there's no 'literal meaning' to unpack, just sound. (An old hanja name 불란서/佛 existed historically but is archaic; nobody uses it now.) The spelling is fixed as 프랑스 and stays identical in casual and formal speech. The language is 프랑스어 (add the usual 어), and a French person is 프랑스 사람 (casual) or 프랑스인 (formal). The main learner pitfall here is spelling and pronunciation: English speakers, influenced by the English 'fr-' sound, sometimes write 후랑스 or 프란스, but the standard form is 프랑스 with 랑 (not 란). Another pitfall is the silent-letter habit — don't try to mirror French/English spelling; Korean writes exactly what is said. Particle behavior is the standard country pattern: 프랑스에 가다 (go to), 프랑스에서 오다/살다 (come from / live in). Don't confuse the country 프랑스 with 불어, an older but still-used alternative name for the French language alongside 프랑스어.

usage: 독일 + 사람 with no particle; means a person from Germany
에서 marks the country of origin
살다 takes location 에 for residence
독일 modifies 자동차; a German-made car
examples: 저는 독일에서 왔어요.
I came from Germany.
Simple origin sentence with 에서
독일 차는 튼튼해요.
German cars are sturdy.
Everyday; 차 = car (short for 자동차), 튼튼하다 = be sturdy
독일에서 엔지니어로 오 년 동안 일했어요.
I worked as an engineer in Germany for five years.

The biggest English-speaker pitfall is reaching for an English-derived word like '저먼' or '게르만' — these are wrong for the country (게르만 refers to the Germanic ethnic/linguistic group, not the modern nation); Koreans always say 독일. Particle behavior is the usual country pattern: 독일에 가다/살다 (go to / live in), 독일에서 오다 (come from). When stating a role, note the example uses 엔지니어로 — the particle (으)로 marks 'in the capacity of', a handy pattern with jobs.

I like foreign food.

외국에 한 번도 안 가 봤어요.
I've never been abroad even once.
Real-situation; 가 보다 = try going/have the experience, 한 번도 + 안 = not even once
nuance: 외국 (外國, 'outside country') is the general word for 'a foreign country / abroad' — the hanja literally combine 外 ('outside') + 國 ('country'), so it means 'any country outside one's own'. Its meaning is relative and speaker-dependent: for a Korean, Japan is 외국, but for a Japanese person, Korea is 외국 — it always means 'not my country'. The key contrast for learners is generality: use 외국 only when you DON'T name a specific country; the moment you mean a particular nation, switch to its name (미국, 일본, etc.). Saying '외국에서 왔어요' is fine if you're being vague ('I came from abroad'), but if you mean the USA, say 미국에서 왔어요. Two important derivatives share the 外國 root: 외국인 (外國人, 'foreigner' — a foreign person) and 외국어 (外國語, 'foreign language'). English speakers sometimes use 외국 where English would say 'overseas' as an adjective, but in Korean 외국 is a noun, so 'go overseas' is 외국에 가다 (literally 'go to a foreign country'). Particle behavior follows the country pattern: 외국에 가다/살다 (go / live), 외국에서 오다 (come from).

usage: 우리 + 나라 written as one word; means one's own nation warmly
어느 = which (among a set); the standard question word for nations
나라 modifies 이름; the name of a country
every country / from country to country
마다 = each/every; common in 나라마다 달라요 'differs by country'
examples: 어느 나라에서 왔어요?
Which country are you from?
Simple, extremely common question; 어느 나라 + 에서 marks origin
우리나라는 사계절이 있어요.
Our country has four seasons.
Everyday; 우리나라 as one word, 사계절 = four seasons
나라마다 인사하는 방법이 달라요.
The way of greeting differs from country to country.
Real-situation; 마다 = each, 다르다 = be different
nuance: 나라 is the plain NATIVE Korean word for 'country' (not Sino-Korean), and it works for any nation in everyday speech. Its closest synonym is the Sino-Korean 국가 (國家), and the dividing line is register and abstraction: 나라 is warm, everyday, and concrete ('어느 나라?'), while 국가 is formal and institutional, used for the state as a political entity (국가 정책 'national policy', 국가대표 'national team' — note 국가 not 나라 here). So you'd ask a new acquaintance 어느 나라에서 왔어요? but a textbook would write 국가 간의 관계 'relations between states'. The single most important collocation is 우리나라 — written as ONE word (not 우리 나라) when it means 'our country' in the sense of 'Korea, from our shared insider view'. English speakers tend to over-use the literal 'my country' (제 나라), which sounds detached; among Koreans the warm default is 우리나라. Particle behavior is regular: 나라가 많다 (there are many countries), 어느 나라에서 (from which country). Don't reach for 국가 in casual conversation — it sounds stiff and bureaucratic.

usage: 한국인 + 이에요; the copula for stating nationality
한국인 modifies 친구; a friend who is Korean
한국인 modifies 관광객; common in travel/news contexts
contrast term sharing the 人 suffix; 외국 + 인 = foreign person
examples: 저는 한국인이에요.
I am Korean.
Simple nationality statement; 한국인 + 이에요
그분은 한국인이 아니에요.
That person is not Korean.
Everyday negation; 이/가 아니다 = is not, 이 marks the subject of the negation
회사에 한국인 동료가 세 명 있어요.
There are three Korean colleagues at my company.
Real-situation; 한국인 modifies 동료, 세 명 counts people
nuance: 한국인 (韓國人, 'Korea-person') means 'a Korean person', built from 한국 + the Sino-Korean suffix 인 (人, 'person'). Its everyday near-synonym is 한국 사람, which means the same thing but feels warmer and more conversational, while 한국인 is slightly more formal and is the form you see in writing, documents, statistics, and news ('한국인 관광객', '재외 한국인'). Both are polite and acceptable — 한국인 is NOT more respectful, just a different register, so don't think you must use 한국인 to be polite. The 인 (人) suffix is productive: 미국인, 중국인, 외국인 all work the same way, paralleling 사람 (미국 사람 etc.). The key English-speaker pitfall is redundancy: because 인 already means 'person', you must NOT say '한국인 사람' — that doubles 'person-person'; choose either 한국인 OR 한국 사람, never both. A second pitfall is the copula: nationality uses 이에요/예요 attached directly (한국인이에요), and the negative is 한국인이 아니에요, with 이 marking the subject of 아니다.

usage: 전 (全, 'all') + 세계; means the entire world, very common
세계 modifies 여행; traveling around the world
세계 modifies 최고; 'best in the world', common in praise/ads
세계 modifies 지도; a map of the world
examples: 저는 세계 여행을 하고 싶어요.
I want to travel the world.
Simple; 세계 여행 as a noun phrase, 을 marks the object of 하다
이 노래는 전 세계에서 유명해요.
This song is famous all over the world.
Everyday; 전 세계 = the whole world, 에서 marks the location of the state
그 회사는 세계 시장에서 경쟁하고 있어요.
That company competes in the world market.
Real-situation; 세계 시장 = world market, 에서 marks the arena of the activity
nuance: 세계 (世界, 'world-realm') means 'the world' as the whole earth and all its countries and peoples — a global, geographic scope. Its tricky near-synonym is 세상 (世上, 'world-above'), and the boundary matters: 세계 is the planet / international sphere (전 세계 'the whole world', 세계 지도 'world map', 세계 평화 'world peace'), whereas 세상 is 'the world' in the sense of human life, society, and 'how things are' (세상이 좋아졌어요 'the world/times have gotten better', 세상 물정 'the ways of the world'). So 'world map' is 세계 지도, never '세상 지도'; but '그런 세상에 살고 싶어요' (I want to live in such a world) uses 세상. The most useful collocation is 전 세계 ('the entire world'), where 전 (全) means 'all'. English speakers who learned 'world' as one word tend to overextend 세계 into the 세상 territory of 'life/society', so anchor it: 세계 = the globe and its nations; 세상 = the human world / life. Particle behavior is regular: 세계가 넓다 (the world is wide), 전 세계에서 (all over the world).

usage: 고향 + 이 + 어디예요; the standard way to ask someone's hometown
내려가다 ('go down') is idiomatic for returning to a hometown outside Seoul
고향 modifies 친구; a friend from where you grew up
고향 modifies 음식; the food of one's home region
examples: 제 고향은 부산이에요.
My hometown is Busan.
Simple; 고향 + 은 topic, 이에요 copula naming the place
명절에 고향에 가요.
I go to my hometown for the holidays.
Everyday; 명절 = traditional holiday, 에 marks the destination
오랜만에 고향에 내려가서 부모님을 뵈었어요.
I went down to my hometown after a long time and saw my parents.
Real-situation; 내려가다 = go down (to one's hometown), 뵈다 = humble 'see/meet' for elders
nuance: 고향 (故鄕, 'old village') means the place where you were born and grew up — the hanja combine 故 ('old/former') + 鄕 ('village/country home'), so it carries a built-in feeling of warmth, nostalgia, and roots, more emotional than the neutral English 'hometown'. It is NOT the same as 집 ('house/home, where you currently live') or 본가 ('one's parents' home'): you can live in Seoul (집은 서울) while your 고향 is Busan. A 고향 can be a city, a town, or a whole region, and it stays your 고향 even decades after you leave. A culturally important collocation is 고향에 내려가다 ('go DOWN to one's hometown') — because Seoul is the center, returning to a provincial hometown is idiomatically 'going down' (내려가다), and going back to Seoul is 올라가다 ('going up'), regardless of actual geography. English speakers often misuse 고향 for their current home or address; remember 고향 is specifically your place of origin and upbringing. The classic conversation opener is 고향이 어디예요? Particle behavior is regular: 고향에 가다 (go to), 고향에서 자라다 (grow up in).
